\chapter{Synthesis --- The Same Conversation, Twice}
\label{ch:synthesis-ar-singular}
\hlchaptermodality{28}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hold one short conversation both warmly and respectfully, changing only the verb ending.}

The register choice carried entirely by one letter - and now with something real to say.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — the same conversation, twice}

\label{lesson:ES-C06-repaso-hablar}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new in this chapter either. This one is for \textbf{using} what you have — because knowing three endings is not the same as choosing the right one while a real person waits for you to finish.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what the ending is really saying}]
You are going to hold one short conversation twice — once with someone your own age, once with someone you want to show respect to. The \textbf{words} barely change. What changes is \textbf{one letter on the end of one verb}.

That letter is the whole message. \emph{Hablas} says \emph{I am at ease with you}. \emph{Habla} says \emph{I am being careful with you}. English would need a change of tone, or a \textquotedblleft{}sir.\textquotedblright{} Spanish does it with an \textbf{-s}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange — with a friend}
\begin{quote}
— ¡Hola! Me llamo Ana. — Me llamo David. Mucho gusto. — ¿\textbf{Hablas} español? — Sí, \textbf{hablo} español. ¡Gracias!
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange, again — being polite}
\begin{quote}
— Buenos días. Me llamo Ana. — Me llamo David. Mucho gusto. — ¿\textbf{Habla} usted español? — Sí, \textbf{hablo} español. Gracias.
\end{quote}

\textbf{One letter.} \emph{Hablas} became \emph{habla}, and the whole exchange changed its temperature. Your own line — \emph{hablo} — never moved, because \emph{you} are still you in both conversations.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item version one, both parts, start to finish
  \item version two — and catch the single letter that moved
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Run whichever version is harder.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the \emph{only} thing that changed between the two conversations? (\textbf{One letter} — \emph{hablas} $\to$ \emph{habla}.) Why did \emph{hablo} stay the same? (Because it is about \textbf{you}, and you did not change.) What does choosing \emph{habla} over \emph{hablas} actually tell the other person? (That you are being \textbf{respectful} — the grammar is carrying the manners.)
\end{tcolorbox}
